rule: English has eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, and interjection. A word's part of speech determines its position and function in a sentence. Some words (e.g. 'work', 'fast') can belong to more than one category depending on use.

examples.text: She sings beautifully.
The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

common_errors.error: I work every day and I like my work.
common_errors.fix: Both sentences are fine — 'work' is a verb in the first and a noun in the second.
common_errors.explanation: Context determines the part of speech, not the word itself.

common_errors: I work every day and I like my work. -> Both sentences are fine — 'work' is a verb in the first and a noun in the second.
tags: parts-of-speech, word-class, basics

rule: A noun names a person, place, thing, idea, or concept. Nouns can be countable or uncountable, singular or plural, common or proper. In a sentence, nouns act as subjects, objects, complements, or objects of prepositions.

examples.text: person, city, book, happiness, information
The teacher gave the student a book.
examples.note: teacher = subject; student = indirect object; book = direct object

common_errors.fix: I bought a book yesterday.
common_errors.explanation: Singular countable nouns need a determiner when mentioned for the first time.

common_errors: I bought book yesterday. -> I bought a book yesterday.

rule: Countable nouns have singular and plural forms and can be counted. They combine with a/an, numbers, many, few, and several. Use singular form with 'a/an' and plural form for more than one.

examples.text: a book / two books
one apple, three apples
several ideas were discussed

common_errors.fix: I have two books.
common_errors.explanation: After numbers and quantifiers like 'two', use the plural form.

common_errors: I have two book. -> I have two books.
tags: noun, countable, plural

rule: Uncountable nouns have no normal plural form and are treated as singular. They combine with much, little, some, and a piece of. Common ones: information, advice, furniture, equipment, luggage, homework, knowledge, news, water, money.

examples.text: some information
a piece of advice
The news is good.

common_errors.fix: a piece of advice / some advice
common_errors.explanation: advice is uncountable; it cannot take 'an' or plural '-s'.

common_errors.fix: much information / a lot of information
common_errors.explanation: information has no plural form.

common_errors: an advice -> a piece of advice / some advice | many informations -> much information / a lot of information

rule: Proper nouns name specific people, places, or things and are capitalized (John, London, Monday, the Internet). Common nouns name general categories (man, city, day, network). Proper nouns usually take zero article unless they are plural place names or official names.

examples.text: I live in Beijing.
the United States

common_errors.fix: I went to London.
common_errors.explanation: Capitalize the pronoun 'I' and proper nouns.

common_errors: i went to london -> I went to London.

rule: Pronouns replace nouns to avoid repetition. Main types: subject (I, you, he, she, it, we, they), object (me, you, him, her, it, us, them), possessive adjective (my, your, his, her, its, our, their), possessive pronoun (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs), reflexive (myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves), and relative (who, whom, whose, which, that).

examples.text: She likes him.
This book is mine.

common_errors.error: Me and John went to the park.
common_errors.fix: John and I went to the park.
common_errors.explanation: Use subject pronouns in subject position; put yourself last.

examples: She likes him. (subject + verb + object pronoun) | This book is mine. (possessive pronoun stands alone)
common_errors: Me and John went to the park. -> John and I went to the park.

rule: Verbs express actions, events, states, or relationships. Main categories: lexical verbs (work, eat, study), auxiliary verbs (be, do, have — used to build tense/negation/questions), and modal verbs (can, could, may, might, must, should, will, would, shall). A finite verb must agree with its subject.

examples.text: She works in a bank.
He is working now.
You must leave.

common_errors.fix: She can swim.
common_errors.explanation: After a modal verb, use the base form.

rule: Adjectives describe nouns or pronouns. They appear before a noun (attributive) or after a linking verb (predicative). They do not change form for plural or gender.

examples.text: a beautiful city
The book is interesting.

common_errors.error: She is a very beauty girl.
common_errors.fix: She is a very beautiful girl.
common_errors.explanation: Use the adjective form 'beautiful', not the noun 'beauty'.

common_errors.fix: These are beautiful books.
common_errors.explanation: Adjectives have no plural form.

examples: a beautiful city (attributive position) | The book is interesting. (predicative after linking verb)
common_errors: She is a very beauty girl. -> She is a very beautiful girl. | These are beautifull books. -> These are beautiful books.
tags: adjective, word-class

rule: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or whole clauses. Common types: manner (quickly, carefully), degree (very, quite), frequency (always, usually), time (yesterday, now), place (here, outside), and sentence adverbs (fortunately, probably).

examples.text: He runs quickly.
She is very happy.
He probably knows the answer.

common_errors.fix: He speaks English well.
common_errors.explanation: Use the adverb 'well' to modify a verb; 'good' is an adjective.

rule: Prepositions show relationships of time, place, direction, manner, and more. They are followed by a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition). English prepositions are highly idiomatic — learn them in combinations rather than translating word-for-word.

examples.text: at 8:00 / on Monday / in August
at the station / on the table / in the room

common_errors.fix: He is good at English.
common_errors.explanation: The adjective 'good' takes 'at' for skill.

common_errors: He is good in English. -> He is good at English.

rule: Conjunctions connect words, phrases, or clauses. Coordinating conjunctions (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so — FANBOYS) join equal elements. Subordinating conjunctions (because, although, if, when, while, unless...) introduce dependent clauses.

examples.text: I wanted to go, but I was busy.
I stayed home because it was raining.

common_errors.error: Because I was tired, so I slept early.
common_errors.fix: Because I was tired, I slept early. / I was tired, so I slept early.
common_errors.explanation: Do not use both 'because' and 'so' in the same clause pair.

rule: Interjections are short exclamations expressing emotion (Oh!, Wow!, Ouch!, Well...). They are set off by commas or exclamation marks and are not grammatically connected to the rest of the sentence.

examples.text: Oh, I see.
Wow! That's amazing!

common_errors.fix: Wow, I can't believe it! / Wow! I can't believe it!
common_errors.explanation: Separate an interjection from the clause.

rule: The basic English sentence pattern is Subject + Verb (S+V). Every complete sentence needs a subject (except imperatives) and a finite verb.

examples.text: Birds fly.
He sleeps.

common_errors.fix: It is raining now.
common_errors.explanation: English usually requires an explicit subject; add a dummy 'it'.

common_errors: Is raining now. -> It is raining now.
tags: sentence-structure, sv

rule: Subject + Verb + Object (S+V+O) is the most common English pattern. The object receives the action of the verb and is usually a noun or pronoun.

examples.text: I like coffee.
She reads books.

common_errors.fix: I like coffee very much.
common_errors.explanation: 'Very' alone cannot modify a verb; use 'very much'.

common_errors: I like coffee very. -> I like coffee very much.
tags: sentence-structure, svo

rule: Subject + Linking Verb + Complement (S+LV+C). Linking verbs (be, become, seem, look, feel, taste, sound) connect the subject to a description; the complement is an adjective or noun, not an adverb.

examples.text: She is happy.
He became a doctor.

common_errors.fix: She looks happy.
common_errors.explanation: After linking verbs use an adjective, not an adverb.

examples: She is happy. (adjective complement) | He became a doctor. (noun complement)
common_errors: She looks happily. -> She looks happy.

rule: Subject + Verb + Indirect Object + Direct Object (S+V+IO+DO). Verbs like give, send, show, tell, buy, bring, teach take two objects. The indirect object can be moved after 'to' or 'for'.

examples.text: She gave me a book.
She gave a book to me.

common_errors.error: She gave to me a book.
common_errors.fix: She gave me a book. / She gave a book to me.
common_errors.explanation: The pattern 'give + to me + noun' is not idiomatic.

common_errors: She gave to me a book. -> She gave me a book. / She gave a book to me.
tags: sentence-structure, ditransitive

rule: Subject + Verb + Object + Object Complement (S+V+O+OC). Some verbs (elect, call, name, make, consider, find) add a complement that describes the object.

examples.text: They elected him president.
We found the movie boring.

common_errors.error: They elected him to be president.
common_errors.fix: They elected him president. / They elected him as president.
common_errors.explanation: Some verbs use a bare noun complement.

common_errors: They elected him to be president. -> They elected him president. / They elected him as president.

rule: The five basic English sentence patterns are: S+V; S+V+O; S+V+LV+C; S+V+IO+DO; S+V+O+OC. Nearly all English sentences are built by extending these five patterns with modifiers and clauses.

examples.text: Birds fly. / I like coffee. / She is happy. / She gave me a book. / They elected him president.

common_errors.error: She gave to me a book last night at the party.
common_errors.fix: She gave me a book last night at the party.
common_errors.explanation: Keep 'give + me + book' together before adding adverbials.

rule: A simple sentence contains one independent clause: one subject + one finite verb (with optional modifiers).

examples.text: I study English.
She and I study English.
examples.note: compound subject is still one clause

common_errors.error: I study English. And I practice every day.
common_errors.fix: I study English, and I practice every day. / I study English and practice every day.
common_errors.explanation: Avoid starting sentences with 'and' in formal writing; it is acceptable informally.

common_errors: I study English. And I practice every day. -> I study English, and I practice every day. / I study English and practice every day.
tags: sentence-types, simple-sentence

rule: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon. Use a comma before the conjunction.

examples.text: I wanted to go, but I was busy.
It was late; we still stayed.

common_errors.error: I was tired, I went home.
common_errors.fix: I was tired, so I went home. / I was tired. I went home.
common_errors.explanation: Two clauses joined only by a comma is a comma splice — a serious error.

rule: A compound sentence joins two or more independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) or a semicolon. Use a comma before the conjunction.
examples: I wanted to go, but I was busy. (coordinating conjunction) | It was late; we still stayed. (semicolon joins clauses)
common_errors: I was tired, I went home. -> I was tired, so I went home. / I was tired. I went home.
tags: sentence-types, compound-sentence, comma-splice

rule: A complex sentence has one independent clause plus one or more dependent clauses introduced by a subordinator (because, although, when, if, while...) or a relative pronoun.

examples.text: I stayed home because it was raining.
The book that I bought is interesting.

common_errors.error: Although it was raining, but we went out.
common_errors.fix: Although it was raining, we went out.
common_errors.explanation: Do not combine 'although' and 'but' in the same sentence.

common_errors: Although it was raining, but we went out. -> Although it was raining, we went out.
tags: sentence-types, complex-sentence, subordination

rule: A compound-complex sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Use it sparingly for clarity.

examples.text: I wanted to go outside, but I stayed home because it was raining.

common_errors.error: When I got home, I was tired, and I went to bed, because it was late.
common_errors.fix: When I got home, I was tired, so I went to bed early.
common_errors.explanation: Too many clauses in one sentence hurts readability; split or simplify.

tags: sentence-types, compound-complex

rule: Present simple form: I/you/we/they + base verb; he/she/it + verb-s/es. Uses: habits, routines, facts, general truths, and fixed schedules.

examples.text: I work every day.
She works every day.
The sun rises in the east.
The train leaves at 6 p.m.

common_errors.fix: She works every day.
common_errors.explanation: Third-person singular present simple takes -s/-es.

rule: Present continuous form: am/is/are + V-ing. Uses: actions happening now, temporary situations, current trends, and fixed near-future arrangements. Do not normally use stative verbs (know, understand, believe, love, own, belong) in the continuous.

examples.text: I am studying now.
She is working from home this week.
We are meeting tomorrow.

common_errors.fix: I know him.
common_errors.explanation: 'know' is stative and is not used in the continuous.

common_errors.fix: He likes coffee.
common_errors.explanation: 'like' is stative in this meaning.

rule: Present perfect form: have/has + past participle. Uses: past action with present relevance, life experience, unfinished time periods (today, this week), and actions continuing until now with for/since.

examples.text: I have finished my work.
She has visited London twice.
I have lived here for five years.

common_errors.fix: I saw him yesterday.
common_errors.explanation: Specific past time expressions (yesterday) require past simple, not present perfect.

common_errors: I have seen him yesterday. -> I saw him yesterday.

rule: Present perfect continuous form: have/has been + V-ing. Emphasizes the duration or ongoing nature of an activity that started in the past and continues (or has just finished with visible effects).

examples.text: I have been studying English for two hours.
You're sweating. Have you been running?

common_errors.error: I have been knowing him for years.
common_errors.fix: I have known him for years.
common_errors.explanation: Stative verbs do not take the continuous, even in perfect continuous.

rule: Past simple form: past form of the verb (worked, went). Use for completed past events, usually with time expressions: yesterday, last week, two days ago, in 2020, at that time.

examples.text: I worked yesterday.
She went home.
They moved to Shanghai in 2020.

common_errors.fix: Yesterday I went to school.
common_errors.explanation: With a past time marker, use the past form, not the base.

rule: Past continuous form: was/were + V-ing. Describes an action in progress at a specific past time, often interrupted by a past simple action.

examples.text: I was studying at 8 p.m.
I was sleeping when he called.
examples.note: long action interrupted by short action

common_errors.fix: When he called, I was sleeping.
common_errors.explanation: Use past continuous for the background action in progress.

rule: Past perfect form: had + past participle. Shows that one past event happened before another past event (the 'earlier of two pasts').

examples.text: When I arrived, she had already left.
He said he had never been to Japan.

common_errors.error: When I arrived, she already left.
common_errors.fix: When I arrived, she had already left.
common_errors.explanation: Use past perfect to mark the earlier event when the sequence matters.

rule: Past perfect continuous form: had been + V-ing. Emphasizes the duration of an activity that was ongoing before a past moment.
examples: She had been working for three hours when I called. (duration before a past point)
common_errors: She was working for three hours when I called. -> She had been working for three hours when I called.
tags: tense, past-perfect-continuous

rule: Future with will: will + base verb. Uses: spontaneous decisions, predictions, promises, and offers.

examples.text: I'll help you.
I think it will rain tomorrow.
Hold on, I'll open the door.

common_errors.fix: I will help you.
common_errors.explanation: 'will' is followed by the base form without 'to'.

metadata.content:

examples: I'll help you. (offer/promise) | I think it will rain tomorrow. (prediction) | Hold on, I'll open the door. (spontaneous decision)
common_errors: I will to help you. -> I will help you.
tags: tense, future, will, prediction

rule: Future with be going to: am/is/are going to + base verb. Uses: plans and intentions, and predictions based on present evidence.

examples.text: I'm going to visit my parents this weekend.
Look at those clouds — it's going to rain.

common_errors.error: I am going to to visit my parents.
common_errors.fix: I am going to visit my parents.
common_errors.explanation: Only one 'to' after 'going'.

common_errors: I am going to to visit my parents. -> I am going to visit my parents.
tags: tense, future, going-to, plans

rule: Future continuous (will be + V-ing) describes an action in progress at a future time. Future perfect (will have + past participle) describes an action completed before a future time.

examples.text: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Paris.
By 2030, she will have finished her PhD.

common_errors.error: By next month, I will work here for two years.
common_errors.fix: By next month, I will have worked here for two years.
common_errors.explanation: For 'by + future time + duration', use future perfect.

examples: This time tomorrow, I will be flying to Paris. (future continuous) | By 2030, she will have finished her PhD. (future perfect)
common_errors: By next month, I will work here for two years. -> By next month, I will have worked here for two years.
tags: tense, future-continuous, future-perfect

rule: Stative verbs describe states rather than actions and are not normally used in continuous forms: know, understand, believe, think (opinion), love, like, hate, want, need, own, belong, seem, mean, prefer, remember. Some verbs have both stative and dynamic meanings (think, have, see, taste).

examples.text: I understand the question.
She owns two cars.
I'm thinking about the problem.

common_errors.error: I am wanting a new phone.
common_errors.fix: I want a new phone.
common_errors.explanation: 'want' is stative.

common_errors: I am wanting a new phone. -> I want a new phone.

rule: Use 'for' + duration (for three years, for two hours) and 'since' + starting point (since 2020, since Monday). Both are commonly used with the present perfect or past perfect.

examples.text: I have lived here for five years.
I have lived here since 2020.

common_errors.error: I have lived here since five years.
common_errors.fix: I have lived here for five years.
common_errors.explanation: 'since' must be followed by a starting point, not a duration.

examples: I have lived here for five years. (for + duration) | I have lived here since 2020. (since + point)
common_errors: I have lived here since five years. -> I have lived here for five years.
tags: tense, for-since, duration

rule: Past simple = finished time, no connection to now (yesterday, last week, in 2020). Present perfect = connection to now or unfinished time (ever, never, just, already, yet, today, this week).

examples.text: I saw that movie last year.
I have seen that movie twice.
examples.note: experience, no specific time → present perfect

common_errors.error: I have seen that movie last year.
common_errors.fix: I saw that movie last year.
common_errors.explanation: 'last year' is a finished-time marker; use past simple.

rule: Present simple = habits and permanent situations. Present continuous = actions in progress now and temporary situations. Time markers help: always/usually/often/every day (simple); now/at the moment/this week (continuous).

examples.text: She works at a bank.
She is working from home this week.

common_errors.fix: I work every day.
common_errors.explanation: 'Every day' marks a habit; use present simple.

common_errors: I am working every day. -> I work every day.

rule: Past simple reports completed short actions; past continuous sets the background scene or describes a longer action in progress. Use 'when' + past simple to interrupt, and 'while' + past continuous for the ongoing action.

examples.text: I was sleeping when he called.
While I was cooking, the phone rang.

common_errors.fix: I was sleeping when he called.
common_errors.explanation: The ongoing action uses past continuous.

rule: Keep tense consistent within a sentence and across a paragraph unless the meaning requires a shift. When reporting past events, keep the whole narrative in past time (but general truths stay present).

examples.text: She opened the door, walked in, and sat down.
He said he was tired.

common_errors.error: Yesterday I went to the store and I buy some milk.
common_errors.fix: Yesterday I went to the store and bought some milk.
common_errors.explanation: Do not shift to present mid-narrative about the past.

rule: Time expressions often determine tense choice: present simple (every day, usually, on Mondays), present perfect (ever, never, just, already, yet, so far, for, since), past simple (yesterday, last week, ago, in + past year), future (tomorrow, next week, soon, in + future time).

examples.text: I haven't finished yet.
She left two days ago.

common_errors.error: I didn't finish my homework yet.
common_errors.fix: I haven't finished my homework yet.
common_errors.explanation: 'yet' typically pairs with the present perfect.

examples: I haven't finished yet. (yet → present perfect) | She left two days ago. (ago → past simple)

rule: A singular subject takes a singular verb; a plural subject takes a plural (base) verb. In present simple, third-person singular adds -s/-es. The verb agrees with the subject, not with nearby words.

examples.text: He works.
They work.

common_errors.error: The list of items are on the table.
common_errors.fix: The list of items is on the table.
common_errors.explanation: The subject is 'list' (singular); ignore the prepositional phrase.

common_errors: The list of items are on the table. -> The list of items is on the table.
tags: subject-verb-agreement, basics

rule: Indefinite pronouns ending in -body, -one, and -thing (everyone, somebody, nobody, anyone, everything, nothing...) are singular. Also singular: each, either, neither.

examples.text: Everyone is ready.
Each student has a book.
Neither answer is correct.

common_errors.fix: Everyone is ready.
common_errors.explanation: 'Everyone' is grammatically singular.

common_errors: Everyone are ready. -> Everyone is ready.

rule: Use 'there is' with a singular noun and 'there are' with a plural noun. The verb agrees with the noun that follows 'there'.

examples.text: There is a problem.
There are two problems.
There is a pen and two books on the desk.

common_errors.fix: There are two problems.
common_errors.explanation: Match the verb to the plural noun.

common_errors: There is two problems. -> There are two problems.

rule: With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the subject closest to it. With 'and', use a plural verb when two subjects are joined (unless they form one unit).

examples.text: Neither John nor his friends are coming.
Either the manager or the assistants handle complaints.
Bread and butter is my favorite breakfast.

common_errors.error: Neither John nor his friends is coming.
common_errors.fix: Neither John nor his friends are coming.
common_errors.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer subject.

examples: Neither John nor his friends are coming. (agree with nearest (friends)) | Either the manager or the assistants handle complaints. (agree with nearest (assistants)) | Bread and butter is my favorite breakfast. (one unit → singular)
common_errors: Neither John nor his friends is coming. -> Neither John nor his friends are coming.
tags: subject-verb-agreement, either-or, neither-nor

rule: Collective nouns (team, family, audience, government, staff, group) are singular in American English; British English allows plural with a plural verb when members act individually.

examples.text: The team is playing well this season.
The team are arguing among themselves.
examples.note: BrE: plural verb for individual members

common_errors.fix: The team is winning. (AmE) / The team are winning. (BrE)
common_errors.explanation: Choose one convention and stay consistent.

rule: Special agreement cases: 'a number of + plural' takes a plural verb; 'the number of + plural' takes a singular verb; fractions/percentages agree with the following noun; titles and names are singular; 'the United States', 'news', 'mathematics' are singular.

examples.text: A number of students are absent.
The number of students is decreasing.
Sixty percent of the work is done.

common_errors.error: The number of students are decreasing.
common_errors.fix: The number of students is decreasing.
common_errors.explanation: 'The number' is the subject and is singular.

rule: Use 'a/an' before singular countable nouns when the listener does not know the specific thing or when it is mentioned for the first time. Choice depends on the SOUND of the next word: 'an' before vowel sounds (an apple, an hour, an honest person), 'a' before consonant sounds (a university, a European, a useful tool).

examples.text: I saw a dog.
an hour
a university

common_errors.fix: an apple
common_errors.explanation: Vowel sound → 'an'.

common_errors.fix: a university
common_errors.explanation: /juː/ is a consonant sound → 'a'.

examples: I saw a dog. (first mention) | an hour ('h' silent → vowel sound) | a university (starts with /juː/ consonant sound)

rule: Use 'the' when the noun is identifiable or specific: already mentioned, unique, made definite by context, or modified by a superlative/ordinal. Also with unique objects, geographical features, and institutions.

examples.text: I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.
Open the door.
the sun / the best / the first / the Internet / the United States

common_errors.error: She is best student in the class.
common_errors.fix: She is the best student in the class.
common_errors.explanation: Superlatives take 'the'.

common_errors: She is best student in the class. -> She is the best student in the class.

rule: Zero article is used with: plural nouns in general statements (Dogs are friendly.), uncountable nouns in general statements (Water is important.), and many proper names (I like music; I live in Beijing). Do not use 'the' for general statements about categories.

examples.text: Dogs are friendly.
Water is important.
She goes to school by bus.

common_errors.error: The dogs are friendly animals. (general statement)
common_errors.fix: Dogs are friendly animals.
common_errors.explanation: General plural statements take zero article.

rule: Many fixed expressions do not follow the general article rules. Zero article: go to school/work/bed/church, by car/bus/train, at home/night, have breakfast/lunch/dinner. With 'the': play the piano/guitar, on the phone, in the morning, go to the movies/the doctor's.

examples.text: I go to school by bus.
She plays the piano.

common_errors.error: I go to the school every day. (as a student)
common_errors.fix: I go to school every day.
common_errors.explanation: Institutional use takes zero article.

examples: I go to school by bus. (zero article) | She plays the piano. (instrument → the)

rule: Countable nouns take a/an, numbers, many, few, several and have plurals. Uncountable nouns take much, little, some and have no plural; use a piece of / a bit of / an item of to count them.

examples.text: a book / two books
a piece of furniture

common_errors.fix: I need some advice. / I need a piece of advice.
common_errors.explanation: 'advice' is uncountable.

common_errors.fix: He gave me a lot of advice. / He gave me several pieces of advice.
common_errors.explanation: 'advice' has no plural; count it with 'pieces of'.

rule: Irregular plurals: man/men, woman/women, child/children, foot/feet, tooth/teeth, mouse/mice, person/people, fish/fish, sheep/sheep, ox/oxen. Foreign plurals: datum/data, medium/media, criterion/criteria, analysis/analyses, phenomenon/phenomena. Nouns ending in -f often change to -ves: leaf/leaves, knife/knives, but roof/roofs, chief/chiefs.

examples.text: one child, two children
The data show a clear trend.

common_errors.error: The sheeps are in the field.
common_errors.fix: The sheep are in the field.
common_errors.explanation: 'sheep' has the same singular and plural form.

rule: 'Many' + countable plural (many books, many people); 'much' + uncountable (much time, much water). In affirmative informal speech, 'a lot of / lots of' is more natural than 'much'. 'How much/how many' ask about quantity.

examples.text: How many books do you have?
How much time do we have?

common_errors.fix: I don't have much money.
common_errors.explanation: 'money' is uncountable → much.

metadata.content:

rule: 'Many' + countable plural (many books, many people); 'much' + uncountable (much time, much water). In affirmative informal speech, 'a lot of / lots of' is more natural than 'much'. 'How much/how many' ask about quantity.
examples: How many books do you have? (many + countable) | How much time do we have? (much + uncountable)
common_errors: I don't have many money. -> I don't have much money.
tags: quantifier, many-much

rule: 'Few' (≈ almost none, negative nuance) vs 'a few' (some, positive nuance) → countable. 'Little' (≈ almost none) vs 'a little' (some) → uncountable.

examples.text: Few people came to the meeting.
A few people came — we can start.
There is little time left.
There is a little time — let's review.

common_errors.error: I have few friends, so I am never alone.
common_errors.fix: I have a few friends, so I am never alone.
common_errors.explanation: 'Few' means almost none; use 'a few' for 'some'.

metadata.content:

rule: 'Few' (≈ almost none, negative nuance) vs 'a few' (some, positive nuance) → countable. 'Little' (≈ almost none) vs 'a little' (some) → uncountable.
examples: Few people came to the meeting. (hardly any) | A few people came — we can start. (some) | There is little time left. (hardly any time) | There is a little time — let's review. (some time)
common_errors: I have few friends, so I am never alone. -> I have a few friends, so I am never alone.
tags: quantifier, few-little, positive-negative-nuance

rule: Use 'some' in affirmative sentences and offers/requests; use 'any' in negatives and questions. 'Some' implies a specific but indefinite amount; 'any' implies an open choice.

examples.text: I have some questions.
Do you have any questions?
Would you like some coffee?

common_errors.fix: I don't have any questions.
common_errors.explanation: Negative sentences take 'any'.

common_errors: I don't have some questions. -> I don't have any questions.

rule: 'A lot of / lots of' work with both countable and uncountable nouns in affirmative speech. 'Plenty of' = more than enough. 'Enough' = sufficient, placed before nouns but after adjectives/adverbs.

examples.text: a lot of books / a lot of time
We have plenty of food.
She is old enough to drive.

common_errors.fix: There is enough time.
common_errors.explanation: 'enough' directly precedes the noun; 'time' is uncountable.

rule: Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) do the action; object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) receive the action or follow prepositions.

examples.text: She likes me.
Between you and me, this is a secret.

common_errors.fix: She likes me.
common_errors.explanation: 'likes' needs an object pronoun.

common_errors.error: Between you and I, this is a secret.
common_errors.fix: Between you and me, this is a secret.
common_errors.explanation: After a preposition, use object pronouns.

rule: Possessive adjectives (my, your, his, her, its, our, their) come before nouns. Possessive pronouns (mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs) stand alone. Do not combine them.

examples.text: This is my book.
This book is mine.

common_errors.fix: This is mine. / This is my book.

rule: Relative pronouns: who (people, subject), whom (people, object, formal), whose (possession), which (things), that (people or things in defining clauses). Choose by whether the antecedent is a person/thing and whether it is subject/object.

common_errors.explanation: Use 'who' for people, 'which' for things.

rule: Modals: can, could, may, might, must, should, ought to, will, would, shall. Structure: modal + base verb (no -s, no 'to' except ought to/have to/be able to). Modals have no -ing or past -ed forms.

common_errors.explanation: After a modal, use the base form — no -s.

common_errors.error: Can I borrow your pen? / May I borrow your pen?
common_errors.fix: Both are fine; 'may' is more formal.
common_errors.explanation: Context and register matter more than strict rules here.

rule: 'Must' = strong obligation from the speaker/rules; 'must not' = prohibition. 'Have to' = external necessity. 'Don't have to' = not necessary (≠ must not!).

common_errors.error: You mustn't come if you don't want to.
common_errors.fix: You don't have to come if you don't want to.
common_errors.explanation: 'Mustn't' = forbidden; 'don't have to' = not necessary.

common_errors.error: That must be true — I'm not sure.

rule: Time prepositions: at + specific time (at 8:00, at noon, at night); on + days/dates (on Monday, on July 5, on my birthday); in + months/years/parts of day/longer periods (in August, in 2026, in the morning, in winter). 'By' = deadline; 'until' = endpoint; 'during' = within a period.

examples.text: The movie is interesting.
I am interested in the movie.

examples.text: small → smaller → the smallest
big → bigger → the biggest
happy → happier → the happiest

common_errors.fix: smaller
common_errors.explanation: Short adjectives take -er, not 'more'.

rule: Equal comparison: as + adjective/adverb + as (as tall as). Unequal: adjective + -er/more ... than (taller than, more expensive than). Negative: not as ... as / less ... than. With multiples: twice as expensive as, three times bigger than.

She is taller than me / than I am.
This phone costs twice as much as that one.

common_errors.error: He is as tall than his father.
common_errors.fix: He is as tall as his father.
common_errors.explanation: Equal comparisons use 'as...as', not 'as...than'.

rule: Passive form: be + past participle. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject; the agent is introduced with 'by' when important. The tense of 'be' carries the time.

examples.text: The company built the house.
The house was built by the company.
English is spoken in many countries.

common_errors.error: The house was build by the company.
common_errors.fix: The house was built by the company.
common_errors.explanation: Passive needs the past participle 'built', not the base.

rule: Use the passive when: the result/object is more important than the agent, the agent is unknown or obvious (My car was stolen.), or the agent is unimportant (The meeting was postponed.). Do not force passive when active is clearer and more natural.

examples.text: The window was broken.
Rice is grown in many countries.

common_errors.error: The meeting was held by the organizers at 3 p.m. yesterday.
common_errors.fix: The organizers held the meeting at 3 p.m. yesterday.
common_errors.explanation: When the agent matters and is clear, active is more natural.

The project has been completed.

rule: 'Get + past participle' is a common informal passive (get married, get hurt, get fired, get dressed). Use 'by + agent' only when the agent adds information; use 'with' for instruments (cut with a knife).

The cake was cut with a knife.
This song was written by Jay Chou.

common_errors.error: The window was broken with my neighbor.
common_errors.fix: The window was broken by my neighbor.
common_errors.explanation: People/agents take 'by'; tools take 'with'.

rule: Yes/No questions invert auxiliary or modal with the subject: (auxiliary/modal) + subject + verb? Use do/does for present simple, did for past simple, be directly for 'be' sentences.

examples.text: Do you like coffee?
Is she working?
Can he swim?
Did you see him?

common_errors.fix: Do you like coffee? / You like coffee? (informal spoken intonation)
common_errors.explanation: Standard written questions invert with 'do'.

rule: WH questions: WH-word + auxiliary + subject + verb? The WH-word is the information gap: what (thing), where (place), when (time), why (reason), who (person), how (manner), how much/many (quantity), how often (frequency).

examples.text: Where do you live?
Why did he leave?
What are you doing?
How often do you exercise?

common_errors.fix: Where do you live?
common_errors.explanation: WH questions require subject-auxiliary inversion (except subject questions).

Which team won?

rule: Choosing question words: which (a limited choice: Which book do you want?), what (open choice: What do you want?), whose (possession: Whose bag is this?), whom (formal object: Whom did you see?), who (object, informal: Who did you see?).

Whose umbrella is this?

common_errors.explanation: Use 'which' for a limited set.

You haven't seen my keys, have you?

common_errors.error: She is coming, isn't she? / She is coming, isn't it?
common_errors.fix: She is coming, isn't she?
common_errors.explanation: The tag pronoun matches the subject.

Do you know where he lives?

common_errors.error: Do you know where does he live?
common_errors.fix: Do you know where he lives?
common_errors.explanation: Indirect questions use statement word order.

rule: Negation: do/does/did + not + base verb (present/past simple); be + not; modal + not + base verb. After the negated auxiliary, the main verb returns to the base form.

examples.text: I do not know.
She does not know.
I did not go.
She is not ready.

common_errors.fix: I didn't go.
common_errors.explanation: After 'didn't', use the base form.

common_errors.fix: She doesn't like it.
common_errors.explanation: Third-person singular negation uses 'doesn't'.

rule: English prefers one negative per clause. Negative words: no, not, never, nobody, nothing, nowhere, neither, none, hardly, scarcely, barely, rarely. Avoid double negatives (not...never, not...nothing).

examples.text: I have never been to Japan.
There is nothing in the box.
She hardly ever complains.

common_errors.fix: I don't have anything. / I have nothing.
common_errors.explanation: Double negatives are non-standard in English (except some dialects).

rule: Zero conditional: If + present, present. Expresses general truths and facts that are always true. 'When' can replace 'if'.

When you boil water, it turns into steam.

common_errors.error: If you will heat ice, it melts.
common_errors.fix: If you heat ice, it melts.
common_errors.explanation: Zero conditional uses present in both clauses.

rule: First conditional: If + present, will + base verb. Real or possible future. Do not normally use 'will' inside the 'if' clause.

If you study hard, you will pass.

common_errors.error: If it will rain, I will stay home.
common_errors.fix: If it rains, I will stay home.
common_errors.explanation: The 'if' clause takes present simple, not 'will'.

common_errors.explanation: Second conditional uses past tense in the 'if' clause.

common_errors.error: If I studied harder, I would have passed.
common_errors.fix: If I had studied harder, I would have passed.
common_errors.explanation: Unreal past needs past perfect in the 'if' clause.

rule: Mixed conditional: If + past perfect, would + base verb (past condition → present result: If I had studied harder, I would be smarter now). Alternatives to 'if': unless (= if...not), as long as / provided that (condition), even if (concession), in case (precaution).

examples.text: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
You can't enter unless you have a ticket.
I'll lend you the book as long as you return it.

common_errors.error: Unless you don't study, you will fail.
common_errors.fix: Unless you study, you will fail.
common_errors.explanation: 'Unless' already contains negation; do not add 'don't'.

rule: Defining relative clauses identify the noun; without them the sentence loses its specific meaning. They take no commas. 'That' can replace who/which in informal defining clauses and can be omitted when it is the object.

examples.text: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
The book (that) I bought is interesting.

common_errors.error: My brother, that lives in Shanghai, is a teacher.
common_errors.fix: My brother, who lives in Shanghai, is a teacher.
common_errors.explanation: 'That' is not used in non-defining clauses; also the commas mark it as non-defining.

rule: Non-defining relative clauses add extra, removable information and are set off with commas. Use who/whom/whose/which — never 'that' — and never omit the relative pronoun.

examples.text: My brother, who lives in Shanghai, is a teacher.
The Eiffel Tower, which is in Paris, attracts millions of tourists.

common_errors.error: The car, that I bought last year, is very reliable.
common_errors.fix: The car, which I bought last year, is very reliable.
common_errors.explanation: Non-defining clauses cannot use 'that'.

rule: Relative adverbs: where (place → the city where I grew up), when (time → the year when we met), why (reason → the reason why I left). They can sometimes be replaced by preposition + which: the city in which I grew up.

examples.text: This is the city where I grew up.
That was the year when we met.
Tell me the reason why you left.

common_errors.error: This is the city which I grew up.
common_errors.fix: This is the city where I grew up.
common_errors.explanation: A place needs 'where' (or in which).

rule: In formal English, prepositions can move before whom/which: the person to whom I spoke, the house in which she lives. In informal English, keep the preposition at the end: the person I spoke to, the house she lives in.

The person I spoke to was helpful.

common_errors.error: The person to who I spoke.
common_errors.fix: The person to whom I spoke. / The person I spoke to.
common_errors.explanation: After a preposition use 'whom' (formal).

metadata.content:
[01 Grammar | relative_preposition_whom_which | level C1]
rule: In formal English, prepositions can move before whom/which: the person to whom I spoke, the house in which she lives. In informal English, keep the preposition at the end: the person I spoke to, the house she lives in.
examples: The person to whom I spoke was helpful. (formal) | The person I spoke to was helpful. (informal/natural)
common_errors: The person to who I spoke. -> The person to whom I spoke. / The person I spoke to.
tags: relative-clause, preposition, whom, formal

rule: The object relative pronoun can be omitted in defining clauses: the book (that) I bought, the man (whom/who) she married. It cannot be omitted when it is the subject: the woman who lives next door (who cannot be dropped).

examples.text: The movie (that) we watched was great.
The woman who lives next door is a doctor.

common_errors.error: The woman lives next door is a doctor.
common_errors.fix: The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
common_errors.explanation: Subject relative pronouns cannot be omitted.

metadata.content:
[01 Grammar | relative_clause_omission | level B1]
rule: The object relative pronoun can be omitted in defining clauses: the book (that) I bought, the man (whom/who) she married. It cannot be omitted when it is the subject: the woman who lives next door (who cannot be dropped).
examples: The movie (that) we watched was great. (object → can omit) | The woman who lives next door is a doctor. (subject → must keep)
common_errors: The woman lives next door is a doctor. -> The woman who lives next door is a doctor.
tags: relative-clause, omission

rule: Coordinating conjunctions join equal elements: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Use a comma before the conjunction when joining two independent clauses.

examples.text: I wanted to go, but I was busy.
She is smart and hardworking.
Hurry up, or you will be late.

common_errors.error: I was tired, I went home.
common_errors.fix: I was tired, so I went home.
common_errors.explanation: Join clauses with a conjunction or split into two sentences — not a comma.

metadata.content:
[01 Grammar | conjunction_coordinating | level A1]
rule: Coordinating conjunctions join equal elements: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so (FANBOYS). Use a comma before the conjunction when joining two independent clauses.
examples: I wanted to go, but I was busy. (contrast) | She is smart and hardworking. (addition) | Hurry up, or you will be late. (alternative)
common_errors: I was tired, I went home. -> I was tired, so I went home.
tags: conjunction, coordinating, fanboys

rule: Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses: because, although/though, if, unless, while, when, before, after, since, until, whereas, as soon as, even though. A dependent clause needs an independent clause to form a complete sentence.

examples.text: Although it was raining, we went outside.
I will call you as soon as I arrive.
He stayed because he wanted to help.

common_errors.fix: Because I was tired, I went to bed early.
common_errors.explanation: A 'because' clause alone is a sentence fragment.

metadata.content:

examples: Although it was raining, we went outside. (concession) | I will call you as soon as I arrive. (time) | He stayed because he wanted to help. (reason)
common_errors: Because I was tired. -> Because I was tired, I went to bed early.
tags: conjunction, subordinating, dependent-clause

rule: Contrast words: although/though/even though + clause; despite/in spite of + noun/-ing; however/nevertheless/on the other hand connect sentences. 'But' joins clauses; 'however' is more formal and follows a period or semicolon.

examples.text: Although it was raining, we went out.
Despite the rain, we went out.
It was raining. However, we still went out.

common_errors.error: Despite it was raining, we went out.
common_errors.fix: Although it was raining, we went out. / Despite the rain, we went out.
common_errors.explanation: 'Despite' takes a noun/gerund, not a clause.

metadata.content:

examples: Although it was raining, we went out. (although + clause) | Despite the rain, we went out. (despite + noun) | It was raining. However, we still went out. (however between sentences)
common_errors: Despite it was raining, we went out. -> Although it was raining, we went out. / Despite the rain, we went out.
tags: conjunction, contrast, although-despite

rule: Cause/result connectors: because/since/as + clause (reason); so/therefore/as a result/consequently (result); so that/in order that (purpose); such...that / so...that (degree result). 'Since' and 'as' are weaker than 'because' and are common at the start of a sentence.

examples.text: She stayed home because she was sick.
It was raining, so we canceled the picnic.
He spoke slowly so that everyone could follow.

common_errors.error: Because it rained, so we canceled.
common_errors.fix: Because it rained, we canceled. / It rained, so we canceled.
common_errors.explanation: Use one connector per cause-result pair.

examples: She stayed home because she was sick. (reason) | It was raining, so we canceled the picnic. (result) | He spoke slowly so that everyone could follow. (purpose)
common_errors: Because it rained, so we canceled. -> Because it rained, we canceled. / It rained, so we canceled.
tags: conjunction, cause-result, so-because

rule: 'Wish' + past simple = unreal present (I wish I knew the answer.); wish + past perfect = past regret (I wish I had studied.); wish + would = desire for change (I wish you would stop.). 'If only' is a stronger version of 'wish'.

examples.text: I wish I knew the answer.
I wish I had studied harder.
If only it would stop raining.

common_errors.error: I wish I know the answer.
common_errors.fix: I wish I knew the answer.
common_errors.explanation: Wish about the present uses past tense.

examples: I wish I knew the answer. (unreal present) | I wish I had studied harder. (past regret) | If only it would stop raining. (desire for change)
common_errors: I wish I know the answer. -> I wish I knew the answer.
tags: subjunctive, wish, if-only, unreal

rule: Verbs of suggestion/requirement (suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, propose) + that + base verb (subjunctive, no -s): 'I suggest that he leave now.' In informal English 'should' is common: 'I suggest that he should leave.'

examples.text: The doctor recommended that she rest.
I insist that he be present.

common_errors.error: I suggest that he leaves now.
common_errors.fix: I suggest that he leave now. / I suggest that he should leave now.
common_errors.explanation: After suggestion verbs, use the base subjunctive.

examples: The doctor recommended that she rest. (bare subjunctive) | I insist that he be present. (subjunctive 'be')
common_errors: I suggest that he leaves now. -> I suggest that he leave now. / I suggest that he should leave now.

rule: 'It's time' + past simple = the time is now (It's time we left.); 'would rather' + past simple = preference about another person (I'd rather you didn't tell him.); 'would rather' + base = preference about yourself (I'd rather stay.).

examples.text: It's time we went home.
I'd rather you stayed.
I'd rather stay at home.

common_errors.fix: It's time we went home.
common_errors.explanation: After 'it's time', use past simple.

metadata.summary: subjunctive it is time would rather
metadata.content:
[01 Grammar | subjunctive_it_is_time_would_rather | level B1]
rule: 'It's time' + past simple = the time is now (It's time we left.); 'would rather' + past simple = preference about another person (I'd rather you didn't tell him.); 'would rather' + base = preference about yourself (I'd rather stay.).
examples: It's time we went home. (past simple after 'it's time') | I'd rather you stayed. (preference about other person) | I'd rather stay at home. (preference about self)
common_errors: It's time we go home. -> It's time we went home.
tags: subjunctive, it-is-time, would-rather

rule: Formal inversion after negative adverbs at the start: Never/Seldom/Hardly/Rarely/Not only/No sooner + auxiliary + subject: 'Never have I seen such a view.' 'No sooner had he left than it started raining.'

examples.text: Never have I seen such a beautiful sunset.
Not only did she win, but she broke a record.

common_errors.error: Never I have seen such a view.
common_errors.fix: Never have I seen such a view.
common_errors.explanation: Negative adverb at the start triggers subject-auxiliary inversion.

rule: Inversion with 'so/such...that' emphasizes degree: 'So tired was she that she fell asleep.' 'Such was the demand that we ran out.' Also inversion after 'only' + adverbial: 'Only then did I understand.'

examples.text: So delicious was the food that we ordered more.
Only after the exam did I realize my mistake.

common_errors.error: Only after the exam I realized my mistake.
common_errors.fix: Only after the exam did I realize my mistake.
common_errors.explanation: 'Only + adverbial' at the start requires inversion.

common_errors: Only after the exam I realized my mistake. -> Only after the exam did I realize my mistake.

rule: Cleft sentences highlight information: 'It was John who broke the vase.' (emphasizes subject); 'What I need is a holiday.' (emphasizes object). Use them for emphasis, not in every sentence.

examples.text: It was yesterday that I heard the news.
What she really wants is a break.

common_errors.error: It was John he broke the vase.
common_errors.fix: It was John who broke the vase.
common_errors.explanation: The cleft needs a relative pronoun after the highlighted noun.

rule: Basic punctuation: end statements with a period, questions with a question mark, strong emotion with an exclamation mark. Capitalize the first word of each sentence and proper nouns.

examples.text: She studies English.
Are you ready?
What a beautiful day!

common_errors.fix: Hello. How are you?
common_errors.explanation: Capitalize sentence-initial words and use sentence punctuation.

rule: Comma rules: separate items in a list (a, b, and c); after introductory elements (However, ..., In 2020, ...); around non-defining clauses; before coordinating conjunctions joining clauses; after 'if/when' clauses at the start. Do NOT join two sentences with only a comma (comma splice).

examples.text: I bought apples, oranges, and bananas.
However, I disagree.
My brother, who lives in Shanghai, is a teacher.

common_errors.error: I was tired, I went home.
common_errors.fix: I was tired, so I went home. / I was tired. I went home.
common_errors.explanation: Comma splice: two independent clauses need a conjunction or a new sentence.

metadata.content:

examples: I bought apples, oranges, and bananas. (list) | However, I disagree. (after introductory) | My brother, who lives in Shanghai, is a teacher. (non-defining clause)
common_errors: I was tired, I went home. -> I was tired, so I went home. / I was tired. I went home.
tags: punctuation, comma, comma-splice

rule: Apostrophes show possession (John's book, the girls' room, the children's toys) and contractions (don't, it's = it is). Do NOT use apostrophes for plural nouns (the 1990s, two CDs, not the 1990's/CD's). 'Its' (possessive) has no apostrophe.

examples.text: Sarah's car
It's raining.
The dog wagged its tail.

common_errors.fix: The dog wagged its tail.
common_errors.explanation: 'It's' = it is; the possessive is 'its'.

metadata.content:

examples: Sarah's car (possession) | It's raining. (it's = it is) | The dog wagged its tail. (its = possessive, no apostrophe)
common_errors: The dog wagged it's tail. -> The dog wagged its tail.

rule: Semicolon joins closely related independent clauses (It was late; we left.); colon introduces lists/explanations (Bring these: a pen, a notebook, and a phone.); quotation marks enclose direct speech ('I'm tired,' she said.).

examples.text: She loves music; he prefers books.
You need three things: patience, practice, and time.
"Let's go," she said.

common_errors.error: Bring these, a pen and a notebook.
common_errors.fix: Bring these: a pen and a notebook.
common_errors.explanation: A colon, not a comma, introduces a list.

metadata.content:

examples: She loves music; he prefers books. (semicolon between clauses) | You need three things: patience, practice, and time. (colon before list) | "Let's go," she said. (quoted speech)

rule: accept (verb) = to take or agree to; except (preposition) = excluding. Remember: 'accept' begins with the sound of 'a', 'except' excludes.

examples.text: I accept your invitation.
Everyone came except John.

common_errors.fix: I accept your apology.
common_errors.explanation: 'Except' means excluding, not receiving.

rule: affect (verb) = to influence; effect (noun) = the result. Exception: 'effect' as a verb is rare and formal (to effect change).

examples.text: The rain affected our plans.

common_errors.explanation: Influence = 'affect' (verb).

rule: beside (preposition) = next to; besides (preposition/adverb) = in addition to / anyway. One 's' = location; two 's' = additional.

Besides math, she studies physics.

common_errors.fix: Beside the window, there is a chair.
common_errors.explanation: Position = 'beside'.

rule: borrow = receive something temporarily (I borrow from you); lend = give something temporarily (I lend to you). Direction is the key.

Can you lend me your pen?

common_errors.error: Can you borrow me your pen?
common_errors.fix: Can you lend me your pen? / Can I borrow your pen?
common_errors.explanation: You lend to someone; you borrow from someone.

tags: vocabulary, confusable, borrow-lend

common_errors.explanation: 'They're' = they are.

rule: tell + person (tell me a story); say + content (say hello); speak/talk = conversation (speak English, talk to a friend). 'Tell' needs an object; 'say' focuses on words.

examples.text: She told me a secret.
He said he was tired.
Can you speak Chinese?
Let's talk about it.

common_errors.fix: She told me a secret. / She said a secret to me (unusual; prefer 'told me').
common_errors.explanation: 'Say' does not take an indirect object person directly.

rule: see = perceive with eyes (see a friend, see a movie — passive); watch = observe over time (watch TV, watch a game); look (at) = direct your gaze (look at the board).

Look at this photo.

common_errors.fix: I watch TV every night.

rule: Everyday alternatives to textbook phrases: 'I'm good' (I'm fine), 'no worries' (you're welcome / it's fine), 'for sure' (certainly), 'sounds good' (that's acceptable), 'my bad' (my mistake, casual), 'no big deal' (not important), 'that works' (that's acceptable).

rule: Natural opinion openers: In my opinion (formal), I think/believe/feel that, As far as I'm concerned, From my perspective, If you ask me (casual), The way I see it. In speech, 'I think' and 'I feel like' dominate.

examples.text: If you ask me, it's a bad idea.
From my perspective, the plan works.

common_errors.fix: In my opinion, ... / As far as I'm concerned, ...
common_errors.explanation: 'According to me' is not idiomatic.

rule: Natural emotion expressions: surprise (No way! / You're kidding! / That's amazing!), happiness (I'm thrilled! / That's great news!), sympathy (I'm sorry to hear that. / That's rough.), frustration (That's so annoying. / I'm fed up with this.).

examples.text: No way! You got the job?
I'm sorry to hear about your loss.

common_errors.error: I am sorry to hear that. (fine) vs 'I pity you.' (wrong nuance)
common_errors.fix: Use 'I'm sorry to hear that' or 'That must be hard.'
common_errors.explanation: 'Pity' can sound condescending in English.

rule: Transition naturally between topics: Anyway, ... (back to main topic); Speaking of..., ... (linked topic); That reminds me, ... ; Before I forget, ... ; On a different note, ... ; Now, let's move on to...

examples.text: Speaking of food, have you tried the new café?
Anyway, back to the report.

common_errors.fix: Vary transitions: 'That reminds me', 'By the way', 'Anyway'.
common_errors.explanation: Repeating one transition sounds mechanical.

rule: Natural emphasis: use stress and intensifiers rather than ALL CAPS: really/so/such/totally (It was so good!), cleft sentences (What I love is...), question tags for agreement (Great view, isn't it?).

examples.text: It was so good!
What I really love is the design.

common_errors.fix: It was absolutely amazing!
common_errors.explanation: Strong adjectives beat repeated 'very'.

rule: Natural frequency expressions: always (100%), usually (90%), normally, often, sometimes (50%), occasionally, rarely/seldom (10%), hardly ever (5%), never (0%). In speech: 'most of the time', 'every now and then', 'once in a while'.

examples.text: I usually walk to work.
We eat out once in a while.

common_errors.fix: I rarely go. / I hardly ever go.
common_errors.explanation: Do not stack contradictory frequency adverbs.

rule: Natural storytelling uses past continuous for background and past simple for main events: 'I was walking home when I saw a dog.' Add time linkers: suddenly, then, after that, eventually, in the end.

examples.text: I was reading when the phone rang.
We waited, and eventually the bus came.

common_errors.error: I was walking home. I was seeing a dog.
common_errors.fix: I was walking home when I saw a dog.
common_errors.explanation: 'See' is not used in continuous here; use past simple for the event.

common_errors.explanation: 'Help' needs 'with' before the thing you need help with.

common_errors.fix: Both correct — 'apologize' is more formal.
common_errors.explanation: Match apology strength to the situation.

rule: Chinglish is English that follows Chinese word order, logic, or collocations rather than English ones. It is usually grammatically understandable but unnatural. Common sources: word-for-word translation, missing English grammatical features (articles, plural -s, tense), and wrong collocations. The cure: learn chunks and collocations, not word-by-word equivalents.

examples.text: I very like English. → I really like English.
Open the light. → Turn on the light.

common_errors.fix: My English is not very good. / I'm still learning English.
common_errors.explanation: Self-deprecation is fine, but 'poor' + 'very' is a direct transfer; softer phrasings are more idiomatic.

rule: Do not translate Chinese word-for-word. Chinese and English grammar differ: articles, tense markers, plural markers, and word order do not align. Translate meaning, not structure.

examples.text: I bought a book yesterday.
我昨天买了一本书 → 'Yesterday I bought a book.'

common_errors.fix: I bought a book yesterday.
common_errors.explanation: Past marker '了' → past tense 'bought'; count requires article/plural.

rule: Chinese has no articles, so Chinese learners often omit them: 'I bought book yesterday.' English requires a/an/the where the noun is singular countable. Use 'a/an' for first mention, 'the' for known/unique.

examples.text: I bought a book yesterday.
She is a teacher.

common_errors.fix: I bought a book yesterday.
common_errors.explanation: Singular countable nouns need a determiner.

common_errors.fix: She is a teacher.
common_errors.explanation: Professions take 'a/an'.

common_errors: I bought book yesterday. -> I bought a book yesterday. | She is teacher. -> She is a teacher.

rule: Chinese nouns have no plural marking, so learners drop English plural -s: 'I have two book.' Use plural forms after numbers, 'many', 'several', and 'a few'.

examples.text: I have two books.
There are many students in the class.

common_errors.fix: I have two books.
common_errors.explanation: Countable nouns take -s after numbers > 1.

rule: Chinese verbs have no person/number inflection, so learners forget third-person -s: 'He like coffee.' Use verb-s/es after he/she/it in present simple.

examples.text: He likes coffee.

common_errors.fix: He likes coffee.
common_errors.explanation: Present simple third-person singular takes -s/-es.

examples.text: Yesterday I went to school.

common_errors.fix: Yesterday I went to school.
common_errors.explanation: Past time words require past verb forms.

rule: Chinese and English word order differ, especially for adverbs, time/place phrases, and questions. English: subject + adverb frequency + verb; time at the end usually. Avoid placing adverbs between verb and object.

examples.text: I always eat breakfast at 7.
She quickly finished the report.

common_errors.fix: I like coffee very much. / I really like coffee.
common_errors.explanation: Do not split verb + object with 'very much'.

examples: I always eat breakfast at 7. (frequency before verb) | She quickly finished the report. (manner before/after verb phrase)

rule: Do not assume one Chinese preposition maps to one English preposition. Chinese '在' can be in/on/at; Chinese '的' can be of/'s. Learn each verb/adjective with its preposition: interested in, good at, depend on.

examples.text: interested in music
married to a doctor

common_errors.fix: interested in music
common_errors.explanation: Fixed collocation: 'interested in'.

common_errors.fix: good at English
common_errors.explanation: Skill → 'good at'.

examples.text: a lot of advice
a piece of information

common_errors.fix: a lot of advice / many pieces of advice
common_errors.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable.

rule: A classic transfer error: 非常喜欢 → 'very like'. English: 'like' is a verb; 'very' modifies adjectives/adverbs, not verbs. Use 'really like' / 'love'.

examples.text: I really like English.
I love this song.

common_errors.fix: I really like English.
common_errors.explanation: 'Very' cannot modify the verb 'like'.

common_errors.error: Although it was raining, but we went out.
common_errors.fix: Although it was raining, we went out.
common_errors.explanation: One conjunction per clause pair.

rule: To reduce Chinglish: (1) learn collocations as chunks (make a decision, heavy rain), not single words; (2) memorize grammar features Chinese lacks (articles, plural -s, third-person -s, tense forms); (3) read/listen to native material and copy patterns; (4) for uncertain sentences, prefer the simplest native structure; (5) run a mental check: 'Would a native speaker say this?'

examples.text: Chunk learning: 'turn on the light', 'do the laundry', 'take a photo'.
Self-check: Would a native say 'very like'? No — 'really like'.

common_errors.fix: Think in English chunks and patterns.
common_errors.explanation: Direct translation is the main source of Chinglish.

Spoken: 'Got it. Thanks!'

common_errors.error: Speaking full textbook sentences in conversation.
common_errors.fix: Use contractions, short answers, and natural intonation.
common_errors.explanation: Over-formal speech sounds unnatural and cold.

rule: In a correction, focus on ONE main error (the most important), not every small issue. State 1-2 additional notes max. Too many corrections overwhelm learners and block acquisition.
examples: 'She go to school yesterday.' → main error: tense (went). Note: subject 'she' fine. (single focus)
common_errors: Listing every error in a long paragraph. -> Prioritize one error; mention others briefly.
tags: ai-rules, feedback-density, pedagogy, policy

rule: Balance correction with praise for what is correct: 'Great sentence! The word order is perfect. Just one small fix: ...' Affirm progress explicitly. Keep tone encouraging, never mocking.

examples.text: 'Good job using present perfect! One detail: we say 'for five years', not 'since five years'.'

common_errors.fix: Acknowledge correct parts first.
common_errors.explanation: Positive reinforcement sustains motivation.

common_errors: Only pointing out errors. -> Acknowledge correct parts first.

rule: If uncertain about a grammar point, say so instead of inventing a rule. Offer: 'I'm not 100% sure, but I believe...' or 'Both forms are used; 'X' is more common in...' Never fabricate grammar rules to sound confident.

examples.text: 'I'm not certain about this one — let me think. I'd say 'who' is fine here.'

common_errors.error: Inventing a false rule with confidence.
common_errors.fix: State uncertainty and give best judgment.
common_errors.explanation: False rules damage trust and learning.

rule: Prefer the smallest correction that fixes the sentence. Only change what is wrong; keep the learner's words, style, and structure when possible. Offer a natural alternative separately when useful.

examples.text: 'I have went to Beijing.' → 'I have been to Beijing.' (minimal fix)

common_errors.fix: Fix the error; keep the learner's voice.
common_errors.explanation: Minimal changes teach precision.

rule: RAG retrieval strategy: (1) embed the user's sentence; (2) retrieve top-k (5-10) chunks by semantic similarity with a hybrid of dense embedding + keyword/tag match; (3) filter by error type inferred from the sentence; (4) rank by level relevance; (5) inject only the most relevant 3-5 chunks into the prompt; (6) treat retrieved rules as candidates, not absolutes.

examples.text: Query: 'She go to school yesterday.' → retrieve tense chunks (past simple, agreement) + chinglish transfer.

common_errors.error: Dumping all 500 chunks into the prompt.
common_errors.fix: Retrieve 3-5 high-quality chunks only.
common_errors.explanation: Precision beats recall for correctness.

rule: The Grammar Validator is a separate LLM pass (or rule engine) that checks the assistant's corrected output BEFORE sending it: verify the correction is itself grammatical, the rule cited exists, the meaning is preserved, and the change is minimal. Output: PASS or FAIL + reason. If FAIL, regenerate.

examples.text: Assistant: 'She goes to school everyday.' Validator: FAIL — 'everyday' is an adjective; use 'every day'.

common_errors.fix: Always validate corrected output.
common_errors.explanation: Self-validation prevents propagating errors.

rule: In multi-turn conversation, track the learner's recurring errors and level. Reuse previous corrections; avoid re-explaining the same rule in the same way (vary examples). If the same error recurs, note the pattern explicitly and suggest targeted practice.

examples.text: Turn 3: 'You used 'since' with a duration again — remember: since + point, for + duration. Let's practice: ...'

common_errors.fix: Carry error history across turns.
common_errors.explanation: Continuity accelerates learning.

rule: After correcting, optionally give a 1-2 sentence micro-lesson: state the rule, give 2 examples, give 1 common error pair. Keep it under 3 sentences unless the learner asks for more.

examples.text: 'Rule: modal + base verb. Examples: can swim, must go. Common error: can swims.'

common_errors.error: Delivering a full grammar lecture after every sentence.
common_errors.fix: Keep micro-lessons short and optional.
common_errors.explanation: Brevity respects the learner's time.

rule: Teach pragmatics alongside grammar: indirect requests (Could you...?), politeness norms (thanks/apologies), small-talk topics to avoid, and register shifts. Pragmatic errors are often more noticeable than grammar errors.

examples.text: 'Give me water' is grammatical but rude; 'Could I have some water, please?' is appropriate.

common_errors.fix: Flag pragmatic issues as 'register/appropriateness'.
common_errors.explanation: Appropriateness is part of fluency.

common_errors.fix: Describe the error, not the person.
common_errors.explanation: Learners need safety to experiment.

rule: LangGraph agent node roles: (1) intent_node — classify task (correct/explain/generate/translate); (2) retriever_node — embed query + fetch top-k chunks from the JSONL vector store; (3) corrector_node — LLM generates correction with retrieved chunks; (4) validator_node — LLM or rule engine verifies correction; (5) explainer_node — builds learner-level explanation; (6) responder_node — formats final reply (text or JSON).

examples.text: graph: intent → retriever → corrector → validator → (loop back to corrector on FAIL) → explainer → responder

common_errors.error: Straight-line pipeline with no validation loop.
common_errors.fix: Add a validator node with a conditional edge.
common_errors.explanation: Validation loops increase output reliability.

rule: When multiple errors exist, teach in this priority: (1) errors blocking meaning, (2) subject-verb agreement, (3) tense/aspect, (4) articles/number, (5) word order, (6) prepositions, (7) collocation naturalness, (8) style. This mirrors the correction priority list and helps learners focus.

examples.text: 'I no go yesterday' → fix negation+tense first ('I didn't go yesterday'), ignore style.

common_errors.fix: Grammar before naturalness.
common_errors.explanation: Foundation errors first.

common_errors.error: Forcing an irrelevant chunk into the answer.
common_errors.fix: Answer from knowledge, be transparent.
common_errors.explanation: Transparency preserves trust.

rule: The core loop of an AI speaking partner: (1) AI prompts the learner (TTS); (2) learner speaks; (3) ASR transcribes the audio; (4) the agent evaluates grammar, naturalness, and pronunciation; (5) AI replies with feedback + next prompt. Budget the loop end-to-end under ~2.5s: parallelize ASR+retrieval, stream the AI reply, and send feedback in chunks (one main point first).

examples.text: AI: 'What did you do last weekend?' → Learner speaks → ASR text → feedback: 'Great! One fix: 'I go' → 'I went'.' → AI: 'And what about this weekend?'

common_errors.error: Feedback after a long silence or a 5s+ pause.
common_errors.fix: Stream feedback and keep pauses short with thinking-time cues.
common_errors.explanation: Latency kills spoken practice flow.

rule: ASR output is noisy: handle homophones, accents, and low confidence. Strategy: (1) keep the raw transcript plus confidence score; (2) when confidence is low, evaluate the most plausible interpretation but state your assumption; (3) distinguish 'learner error' from 'ASR error' — if the transcript is clearly garbled, ask a clarification or offer the likely sentence for confirmation instead of correcting grammar.

examples.text: ASR: 'I goed to park.' → low confidence on 'goed' → treat as intended 'went', correct gently.
ASR: 'bafroom' for 'bathroom' → confirm: 'Did you mean bathroom?'

common_errors.error: Correcting grammar that exists only in the ASR transcript, not in the speech.
common_errors.fix: Verify with confidence scores or ask for confirmation.
common_errors.explanation: Correcting ASR noise confuses learners.

rule: Pronunciation feedback has four dimensions: accuracy (phoneme-level: th/r/l/v/w), fluency (speed, pausing, chunking), completeness (words covered), and prosody (stress, rhythm, intonation). Give 1-2 concrete, imitable tips per turn — point to the exact syllable, not abstract scores. Offer a shadowing mode for problem words.

examples.text: Feedback: 'The word 'world' — the /r/ after /w/ needs a slight curl. Try: wor-ld.' + playback comparison.
Fluency note: 'Try pausing between phrases, not inside: I usually get up / at seven.'

common_errors.error: Showing only a 0-100 score with no actionable tip.
common_errors.fix: Always attach one concrete, imitable action.
common_errors.explanation: Scores without guidance don't improve speech.

rule: Roleplay framework for scenario practice: (1) scene card — setting, roles, goal (e.g. 'At a café: order a drink and ask for the bill'); (2) target language — useful collocations and chunks for the scene; (3) the AI plays the other role and stays in character; (4) difficulty scaling — add unexpected turns as the learner improves. After the scene, debrief: 2-3 golden phrases the learner used or missed.

examples.text: Scene: 'Hotel check-in'. AI: 'Good evening, do you have a reservation?' Learner: 'Yes, under the name Li.'
Debrief: 'Great job! A natural alternative for 'I want a room': 'I'd like a room for two nights.'

common_errors.error: Breaking character to give a long grammar lecture mid-scene.
common_errors.fix: Stay in character; save detailed teaching for the debrief.
common_errors.explanation: Immersion builds fluency; analysis breaks it.

rule: Handle interruptions and silence: (1) VAD detects the learner stopped speaking (endpointing); (2) barge-in — learner can interrupt the AI's reply, so the AI should stop TTS promptly; (3) on prolonged silence, offer a hint or rephrase the question, not a new question; (4) on overlapping speech, give the learner the floor.

examples.text: Silence 3s → AI: 'Take your time. A hint: we use 'since' with a point in time...'
Learner interrupts mid-answer → AI stops TTS and listens.

common_errors.error: Talking over the learner or restarting the topic on silence.
common_errors.fix: Stop speaking, yield the floor, prompt with a hint.
common_errors.explanation: Turn-taking politeness is core to spoken UX.

rule: Scale scenario difficulty deliberately: easy (repeating model sentences, Q&A on familiar topics: family, daily routine) → medium (opinions, narration, roleplay with 2-3 turns) → hard (debate, storytelling, hypothetical questions, roleplay with unexpected events). Track which scenario types the learner has mastered; do not repeat the same scene verbatim.

examples.text: A1: 'Do you like tea or coffee?' → B1: 'Tell me about your daily routine.' → C1: 'How would you handle a difficult customer at work?'

common_errors.error: Jumping to abstract topics for beginners.
common_errors.fix: Start with concrete, personal, high-frequency topics.
common_errors.explanation: Familiar content reduces cognitive load for speaking.

rule: Manage turn-taking explicitly: the AI signals when it's the learner's turn (rising intonation in TTS, explicit cues: 'What do you think?', 'Your turn.'), respects a configurable response window, and after the learner's turn confirms receipt ('Got it.') before feedback. For low levels, model the answer first, then ask the learner to say it.

examples.text: AI: 'I usually get up at seven. How about you?' → learner turn → AI: 'Nice, thanks for sharing! One tiny fix: ...'

common_errors.error: The AI answering its own questions or interrupting the learner's turn.
common_errors.fix: Explicitly yield the floor and wait.
common_errors.explanation: Turn cues are the rhythm of conversation.

rule: Normalize repair strategies (self-correction and clarification), and explicitly reward them: when the learner self-corrects ('...I mean, I went'), praise it — self-repair is a strong fluency marker. When the learner asks for help mid-sentence ('how do you say...?'), answer instantly with the word and let them continue.

examples.text: Learner: 'I go — I mean, I went shopping.' → AI: 'Excellent self-correction! That's exactly what fluent speakers do.'
Learner: 'How do you say 收据?' → AI: 'Receipt. Say it: receipt. Now continue your story!'

common_errors.fix: Treat repair and reformulation as progress.
common_errors.explanation: Repair strategies are part of communicative competence.

rule: In spoken practice, correction priority differs from writing: (1) errors that block understanding (highest), (2) high-frequency errors the learner makes repeatedly, (3) pronunciation of key words, (4) grammar details, (5) style. In ONE turn, correct only ONE main point — for speech, prefer immediate correction of a blocking error, and defer minor issues to a summary at the end.

examples.text: Learner: 'I go cinema yesterday and see my friend.' → immediate fix: 'I went to the cinema yesterday...' (meaning-critical), note 'saw' at the end.

common_errors.error: Interrupting the learner to fix every error while they are speaking.
common_errors.fix: Let them finish; fix one blocking error; summarize the rest.
common_errors.explanation: Frequent interruptions destroy speaking flow.

rule: Pronunciation coaching content: (1) phoneme accuracy — common L1 problem sounds (e.g. Chinese learners: th, final consonants, l/r, v/w, long/short vowels); (2) word stress — re-SPECT, PHO-to-graph vs pho-TOG-raphy; (3) sentence stress and weak forms — function words reduce ('to' → /tə/); (4) linking and rhythm — 'not_at_all', consonant+vowel linking; (5) intonation — rising for questions, falling for statements. Use minimal pairs and shadowing drills.

examples.text: Minimal pair drill: 'ship' vs 'sheep' — 'The ship is on the sea. The sheep is on the hill.'
Stress tip: 'PHO-to-graph' (noun) vs 'pho-TOG-ra-pher' (person).

common_errors.error: Coaching only segmental sounds and ignoring stress/rhythm/intonation.
common_errors.fix: Layer: phonemes → stress → weak forms → linking → intonation.
common_errors.explanation: Prosody carries most of the 'native-like' impression.
