rule: Build a learner profile: (1) estimated CEFR level per skill (speaking vs writing often differ); (2) error profile — histogram of error types from all past turns (tense? articles? word order?); (3) vocabulary range; (4) preferred topics and weak scenario types; (5) correction sensitivity — some learners want full correction, others only blocking errors (ask!). Persist the profile per user and update it incrementally after each session.

common_errors.error: Treating every session as the first — same level, same errors, same topics.
common_errors.fix: Load the profile and tailor level, errors, and scenarios.
common_errors.explanation: Personalization is the main value of a practice partner.

rule: Apply spaced repetition to errors: after a corrected error, schedule a re-test in the same session (1-2 turns later), then next session, then +2 sessions, etc. Keep a small queue of 'due errors' (max 3) and weave them into new scenarios naturally rather than drilling in isolation.

examples.text: Turn 5: learner misused 'since + duration' → fix. Turn 7: scene includes 'I have lived here ___ 2019' → natural re-test. Next session: opener includes a 'for/since' prompt.

common_errors.fix: Schedule due errors into future turns.
common_errors.explanation: Spaced retrieval converts correction into acquisition.

rule: Stream AI replies (SSE or WebSocket): first send the correction + reason immediately (the 'what'), then stream the explanation and examples (the 'why'), then the next prompt. This matches spoken UX — learners need instant closure on their error, not a wall of text. Chunk size per SSE event: 1-2 sentences.

examples.text: Event 1: 'Great job!' → Event 2: 'One fix: went, not go.' → Event 3: 'Because yesterday is past...' → Event 4: 'Now tell me about your weekend plans!'

common_errors.error: Streaming a 300-word lecture before any feedback.
common_errors.fix: Feedback first, explanation second, next prompt last.
common_errors.explanation: Instant closure keeps the learner engaged.

rule: Spoken practice latency budget: ASR ~0.5s (streaming ASR), intent+retrieval ~0.2s (parallelize embedding search with ASR finalization), LLM first token <1s (streaming), TTS first frame <0.3s. Total perceived wait under ~2s. Engineering: pre-fetch likely chunks during ASR, cache embeddings, keep LLM prompts small, and reuse warm connections.

examples.text: Pipeline: learner stops speaking → ASR finalizes (0.5s) → retrieval already warmed (0.1s) → LLM streams first token (0.8s) → TTS starts (0.2s).

common_errors.error: Sequential, non-overlapping stages adding up to 5s+.
common_errors.fix: Overlap retrieval with ASR; stream everything.
common_errors.explanation: Latency is the #1 spoken-UX killer.

rule: Design for motivation: (1) praise specific behavior, not generic ('Your intonation on questions was spot-on today' beats 'Good job'); (2) show progress — error-type counts dropping, words learned, scenarios unlocked; (3) keep streaks gentle — never shame a missed day; (4) offer challenge tiers and badges per scenario; (5) end sessions on a win and a concrete 'next step'.

examples.text: Session end: 'Today you spoke for 12 minutes, used 3 new collocations, and fixed the past-tense pattern twice. Tomorrow: the café scene!'

common_errors.error: Focusing the recap on mistakes made.
common_errors.fix: Frame progress + one concrete next step.
common_errors.explanation: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness sustain practice.

rule: Voice data is sensitive: (1) obtain explicit consent for recording; (2) prefer streaming/stateless ASR — do not store raw audio unless the user opts into review history; (3) if stored, encrypt at rest, offer delete-everything, and cap retention; (4) for minors, require guardian consent and disable open-ended topics; (5) run content safety on both ASR text and AI replies; (6) never train on user audio without explicit opt-in.

examples.text: Policy defaults: audio processed in memory, transcripts stored (user-visible), raw audio TTL 24h, one-tap 'erase my voice data'.

common_errors.error: Storing all recordings indefinitely without consent.
common_errors.fix: Minimize, encrypt, expire, and disclose.
common_errors.explanation: Trust is the foundation of a voice companion.

rule: Graceful degradation for voice failures: (1) ASR error/low confidence → confirm with the learner or fall back to text input; (2) TTS failure → render text; (3) network drop → resume with the last state (do not restart the scenario); (4) silence repeatedly → switch to a typing response and offer a simpler question; (5) always keep a text-mode equivalent of the flow so the product works without voice.

examples.text: ASR times out twice → AI: 'I couldn't catch that. You can also type it — or shall we try an easier question?'

common_errors.error: Failing hard or losing conversation state on a voice error.
common_errors.fix: Preserve state; degrade one layer at a time.
common_errors.explanation: Voice adds value only when it never blocks learning.

rule: Close the feedback loop: (1) let learners rate each correction (helpful / confusing / wrong); (2) flag validator failures for weekly review — high FAIL rates on a chunk signal bad knowledge or bad phrasing, then edit build/data_*.py and regenerate; (3) A/B test correction density (one-error vs two-error feedback); (4) track retention — do learners stop making the corrected error in later sessions? That is the real KPI.

examples.text: Metric board: validator FAIL rate per chunk, correction helpfulness %, error recurrence rate after 7 days, session length, scenario completion.

common_errors.error: Shipping corrections with no measurement of learning effect.
common_errors.fix: Measure error recurrence, not just correction count.
common_errors.explanation: Correction quality = learning outcome, not output volume.

rule: Everyday greetings beyond 'How are you?': 'How's it going?', 'How are you doing?', 'What's up?', 'Long time no see!', 'Good to see you!'. Answer naturally: 'Pretty good.', 'Not bad.', 'Can't complain.', 'Same as usual.', 'Busy as always!'. Reply back with 'And you?' or 'How about yourself?'.

examples.text: A: How's it going? B: Pretty good, thanks. You?
A: Long time no see! How have you been? B: I've been busy. How about you?

common_errors.error: A: How are you? B: Fine, thank you, and you?
common_errors.fix: A: How's it going? B: Pretty good, you?
common_errors.explanation: 'Fine, thank you, and you?' is a textbook template; native speakers mix it up naturally.

A: It's pouring. Did you bring an umbrella? B: No, I'm soaked!

common_errors.fix: It's raining today.
common_errors.explanation: Weather uses 'it' as the subject in English.

common_errors.fix: Wash your hands.

rule: 'Sleep in' = sleep late in the morning (sleeping in). 'Stay up late' = go to bed late at night. Both are different from Chinese '睡懒觉/熬夜' mixing.

I stayed up late watching the game last night.

common_errors.error: I sleep late on weekends. (meaning: sleep in)
common_errors.fix: I sleep in on weekends.
common_errors.explanation: 'Sleep late' is ambiguous; 'sleep in' clearly means staying in bed longer.

rule: Short natural answers make speech flow: Yeah / Uh-huh / Not really / Sort of / Kind of / You bet / No way / Totally / I guess so / I don't think so. Use them as replies to yes/no questions instead of full sentences.

common_errors.error: A: Are you free tomorrow? B: I am free. (stiff)
common_errors.fix: Yeah, I'm free. / Sure, I am.
common_errors.explanation: Full repeated sentences sound robotic; short answers are natural.

common_errors.fix: React: 'Oh really?' / 'That's cool!' / 'And then?'
common_errors.explanation: Active listening responses are expected in English conversations.

common_errors.fix: I'd love to, but I can't this time.
common_errors.explanation: Bare 'no' sounds rude; soften with 'I'd love to, but...'.

common_errors.fix: Pick ONE small word per sentence.
common_errors.explanation: Over-stuffing small words sounds messy; use them sparingly.

rule: Daily speaking mode: the conversation itself is the product, correction is a service. Default posture: (1) keep the chat going — ask one follow-up question per turn; (2) correct only ONE main error per turn, after praising; (3) prefer 'recast' (quietly say the correct version) over grammar lectures; (4) if the learner is flowing, do not interrupt — save notes for the end of the session.

examples.text: Learner: 'I go to gym yesterday.' AI: 'Nice! Did you go to the gym alone? — and I'd say: I went to the gym yesterday.'

common_errors.error: Lecture: 'Yesterday requires past simple tense...' mid-conversation
common_errors.fix: Recast: 'I went to the gym — did you enjoy it?'
common_errors.explanation: Recasts keep the conversation flowing while modeling the fix.

rule: For Chinese learners in daily speaking, prioritize these error families in order: (1) errors that block meaning; (2) missing past tense markers (go→went, eat→ate); (3) missing third-person -s; (4) missing/dropped articles (a/the); (5) literal Chinglish translations (very like, open the light); (6) wrong prepositions. Fix these before style issues like wordiness.

examples.text: Learner: 'He go to school every day and yesterday he eat rice.' → fix 'goes' (habit) and 'ate' (past) as two separate turns; don't tackle both at once.

common_errors.error: Correcting word order/style before the tense error.
common_errors.fix: Fix the meaning-blocking or high-frequency error first.
common_errors.explanation: Priority = meaning > frequency > grammar detail > style.

rule: Support Chinese-English mixed input: when the learner types/speaks Chinese (e.g. '我昨天去公园了，很好玩'), (1) reply in English; (2) briefly show the natural English version ('I went to the park yesterday. It was fun!'); (3) ask one follow-up in English. This bridges meaning-first learners into English output.

examples.text: Learner: '我想点一杯咖啡' → AI: 'Got it! In English: I'd like a coffee, please. What size would you like — small, medium, or large?'

common_errors.error: Replying in Chinese to Chinese input.
common_errors.fix: Always respond in English; model the sentence; keep prompts in English.
common_errors.explanation: The product goal is spoken English output, so English is the only reply language.

rule: Turn length balance for daily practice: AI replies should be 2-4 sentences (a reaction + a correction/recast + one follow-up question). Learner turns are naturally 1-3 sentences. If the learner writes a long paragraph, respond to ONE point and ask about another.

examples.text: Good AI turn: 'That's great progress! One small fix: we say 'I've been to' for experiences — I've been to Shanghai twice. How about you — where have you been?'

common_errors.fix: Keep it to 2-4 sentences: react, fix one thing, ask one question.
common_errors.explanation: Short turns keep the dialogue alive and give the learner space to speak.

rule: Anchor teaching to the current scenario: when the learner is in a café scene, teach café sentences ('I'd like a latte'), when in a taxi scene, teach transport chunks. Only bring in off-scene grammar when it blocks the current exchange.

examples.text: Scene = coffee shop. Learner says 'I want coffee.' → AI: 'Perfect place to learn: I'd like a coffee — that's the natural way to order here!'

common_errors.error: Teaching random grammar unrelated to the current scene.
common_errors.fix: Use the scene's high-frequency phrases as the teaching material.
common_errors.explanation: Scene chunks stick better because the learner needs them right now.

rule: In voice-based daily practice, feedback must be speakable: (1) give the corrected sentence OUT LOUD (model it) so the learner can repeat; (2) keep explanation to one short clause ('we use 'went' for yesterday'); (3) after correction, invite a retry: 'Can you say that again?' or 'Now you try.'

examples.text: AI: 'Almost! For yesterday we say 'went' — I went to the store. Can you try that sentence?'

common_errors.error: Writing-style feedback: 'The past simple of go is went, see grammar rule 42.'
common_errors.fix: Speak the model sentence and invite an oral retry.
common_errors.explanation: Voice practice needs spoken models, not written rules.
